title: Avoiding Online Scams and Fraud
objectives: Recognise common online and phone scams that target people, including newcomers
Learn the warning signs of a scam and how to protect your money and information
Know what to do if you are targeted or have already been tricked
Use warning and advice language (if..., make sure, be careful not to)

reading_passage.title: Spotting a Scam Before It's Too Late
reading_passage.text:
Scams — dishonest schemes designed to trick people out of money or personal information — are common, and they can target anyone. Newcomers to a country can be especially at risk, because they may be unsure of how official systems really work. The best protection is knowledge: once you understand how scams operate, they become much easier to spot and avoid.

Most scams share a small number of warning signs, and learning these is more useful than memorising every trick. First, scammers create a sense of urgency: they say you must act right now, or something terrible will happen — you will be arrested, deported, or lose your money. This pressure is designed to stop you thinking clearly. Second, they ask for money or personal information in unusual ways: by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency, or they ask for your bank details, passwords, or Social Security number. Third, the contact is often unexpected, and the story does not quite make sense when you look closely. If any of these signs appear, be very careful.

Some scams are worth knowing by name because they are so common. In the government imposter scam, someone calls pretending to be from the tax office, immigration, or the police, and demands immediate payment to avoid arrest or deportation. Remember: real government agencies do not call and demand payment by gift card, and they do not threaten immediate arrest over the phone. In the prize scam, you are told you have won a lottery or prize, but must pay a fee to receive it — a real prize never requires a payment. In phishing, a fake email or text pretends to be from your bank or a company and asks you to click a link and enter your details. Always go to a company's website directly instead of clicking links in unexpected messages.

Protecting yourself comes down to a few firm habits. Never send money or give personal information to someone who contacted you unexpectedly, no matter how urgent or official they sound. Do not click links in unexpected emails or texts. If someone claims to be from an organisation, hang up and call the organisation back using a number you find yourself, not one they give you. And be especially careful with anyone who asks to be paid in gift cards or wire transfers — these are favourite methods of scammers precisely because they are almost impossible to trace or recover.

If you are targeted, or realise you have been tricked, do not be ashamed — scams fool millions of sensible people every year. Act quickly. Contact your bank if you have sent money or shared account details; sometimes a payment can still be stopped. Change any passwords that may have been exposed. Report the scam to the authorities, such as the Federal Trade Commission, which tracks scams and can advise you. And warn friends and family, because scammers often target the same communities. Knowledge, shared, is the strongest protection of all.

glossary.meaning: a dishonest scheme designed to trick people out of money or information
a feeling that something must be done immediately
a scam using fake emails or texts to trick you into giving personal details
a person who pretends to be someone else in order to deceive

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what are the three common warning signs of a scam?
comprehension.answer: First, a sense of urgency — you must act right now or something terrible will happen. Second, a request for money or personal information in unusual ways (gift card, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or asking for bank details, passwords, or Social Security number). Third, unexpected contact with a story that does not quite make sense on closer inspection.

comprehension.question: Why do scammers create a sense of urgency, according to the passage?
comprehension.answer: Because the pressure 'is designed to stop you thinking clearly.' If a person feels they must act immediately to avoid disaster, they are less likely to pause, question the story, or check with someone — which is exactly what would reveal the scam.

comprehension.question: What is 'phishing', and how does the passage say you should protect against it?
comprehension.answer: Phishing is a scam using a fake email or text that pretends to be from your bank or a company and asks you to click a link and enter your details. To protect yourself, the passage advises always going to a company's website directly instead of clicking links in unexpected messages.

comprehension.question: Why does the passage say to call an organisation back using a number you find yourself?
comprehension.answer: Because a scammer pretending to be from an organisation will give you a fake number that connects back to them. Finding the real number independently (for example, on the organisation's official website) ensures you reach the genuine organisation, not the scammer.

language_focus.title: Giving Warnings and Advice: if..., make sure, be careful not to
language_focus.explanation: To warn and advise, English uses several forms. 'If...' + advice describes a situation and what to do: 'If someone demands a gift card, hang up.' 'Make sure (that)...' gives strong advice to do something important: 'Make sure you call the real number.' 'Be careful not to...' warns against a specific action: 'Be careful not to click the link.' 'Never...' gives the strongest warning.

examples.sentence: If someone asks you to pay with a gift card, be careful — it's almost always a scam.
examples.note: 'If...' sets up the situation; 'be careful' warns; the reason follows.

examples.sentence: Make sure you never share your password, and be careful not to click links in unexpected texts.
examples.note: 'Make sure you never...' is a strong instruction; 'be careful not to...' warns against a specific action.

practice.sentence: Give a warning with 'be careful not to': clicking links in strange emails.
practice.answer: Be careful not to click links in strange emails.

practice.sentence: Give advice with 'if': someone claims to be from the bank and asks for your password.
practice.answer: If someone claims to be from the bank and asks for your password, hang up and call the bank yourself.

practice.sentence: Give strong advice with 'make sure': using a number you find yourself.
practice.answer: Make sure you call back using a number you find yourself.

speaking_task.context: A friend tells you they got a phone call from someone claiming to be from the tax office, saying they owe money and will be arrested today unless they pay with gift cards. Your friend is frightened.
speaking_task.prompt: Reassure your friend and advise them what to do. Explain why this is a scam, and tell them what to do next. Use warning and advice language (if..., make sure, be careful not to, never). Speak for about ninety seconds.
useful_language: Don't worry — this is a very common scam.
Real government offices never demand payment by gift card.
Make sure you don't send them any money.
If they call again, just hang up.
Be careful not to give them any personal information.
speaking_task.model_answer: Okay, first, don't panic — this is a very common scam, and a lot of people get this exact call. The tax office would never phone and demand payment by gift card, and they would never threaten to arrest you today over the phone. That's how you know it's fake. So, make sure you don't send them any money, and be careful not to give them any personal information — not your bank details, not your Social Security number, nothing. If they call again, just hang up. If you want to be completely sure, we can look up the real tax office number together and call them ourselves to check. And it's a good idea to warn your family, because scammers often try the same trick on lots of people in the same community. You did the right thing telling me.

writing_workshop.task: Write a short warning message for a community group chat, alerting people to a scam that is going around and telling them how to protect themselves. Include the warning signs and clear advice.
writing_workshop.model_text:
IMPORTANT — PLEASE READ AND SHARE

Several people in our community have received scam phone calls this week. The caller pretends to be from immigration or the tax office and says you will be arrested or deported today unless you pay immediately with gift cards. Please know: this is a scam. Real government offices never call to demand payment by gift card, and they never threaten immediate arrest over the phone. If you get a call like this, do not panic and do not pay. Never give your personal details or bank information. Be careful not to trust the number they give you — hang up and, if you want to check, call the real office using a number you find yourself. Please share this with your family and neighbours, especially older relatives, so no one is tricked. Stay safe.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: The message names the specific scam, states clearly that it is fake and why, and gives direct advice using warning language ('never give', 'be careful not to', 'do not pay'). Asking readers to share it, especially with vulnerable relatives, reflects the reading's point that shared knowledge is the strongest protection.
success_criteria: Describe the specific scam and its warning signs
State clearly that it is a scam and why
Give direct advice using warning language
Ask readers to share the warning

listening_exercises.transcript: Caller: Hello, this is Officer Johnson from the Immigration Department. Our records show a serious problem with your file. There is a warrant for your arrest. Resident: What? I don't understand. Caller: You must act now. To cancel the warrant, you need to pay a fine of two thousand dollars today, using gift cards. If you do not, officers will come to arrest you within the hour. Do not tell anyone. Resident: This... this doesn't sound right. Immigration wouldn't ask for gift cards. Caller: This is a special emergency process. You must go to the store now and buy the cards. Resident: No. Real government offices never demand gift cards or threaten arrest over the phone. I'm going to hang up and call the immigration office myself using their official number. Caller: If you hang up, you will be arrested — Resident: Goodbye. [hangs up] I'm going to report this call and warn my family.
listening_exercises.question: How does the resident correctly identify the call as a scam?
options: Real government offices never demand gift cards or threaten arrest by phone
The caller had the wrong name

listening_exercises.transcript: Friend 1: I got a text saying I won a five-hundred-dollar gift card, but I have to pay a twenty-dollar 'delivery fee' to claim it. Should I? Friend 2: No, definitely not. That's a classic prize scam. A real prize never asks you to pay a fee to receive it. Friend 1: But it looked official, with a company logo and everything. Friend 2: Scammers copy logos all the time. Be careful not to click any link in that text, and don't give them any card details. If you paid the twenty dollars, they'd just ask for more, and you'd never get a prize. Friend 1: That makes sense. I almost did it — it seemed real. Friend 2: Don't feel bad, these tricks fool lots of people. Just delete the text. And if you're ever unsure, ask me before you pay anything. Friend 1: I will. Thanks for stopping me. Friend 2: Any time. Better to check first than lose your money.
listening_exercises.question: Why does Friend 2 say the prize text is a scam?
options: The gift card is too small
A real prize never asks you to pay a fee to receive it
